mcqs.q: The SI unit of force is:
mcqs.explanation: Force = mass × acceleration → kg·m/s², named the newton (N). Joule is energy, watt is power, pascal is pressure.

mcqs.q: 'To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction' is Newton's:
mcqs.explanation: Third law of motion — rockets, gun recoil and walking all use it.

mcqs.q: A body covers 60 metres in 12 seconds. Its average speed is:
The work done by a force acting perpendicular to the displacement is:
mcqs.explanation: W = F·s·cosθ; at θ = 90°, cos90° = 0 → work = zero (e.g., carrying a bag while walking level).

mcqs.q: The energy stored in a stretched rubber band is:
mcqs.explanation: Energy stored due to position/shape is potential energy (elastic PE here).

mcqs.q: An object weighing 60 N on Earth would weigh on the Moon (g = g/6):
mcqs.explanation: Weight = mg; with g/6, weight = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 N (mass unchanged).

mcqs.q: The SI unit of work is:
mcqs.explanation: Joule (J) = N·m = kg·m²/s².

mcqs.q: The SI unit of power is:
mcqs.explanation: Watt (W) = Joule/second.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
mcqs.explanation: Velocity has both magnitude and direction — vector. Speed is scalar.

mcqs.q: Newton's first law of motion is also called:
mcqs.explanation: First law = Law of Inertia — a body continues in its state unless acted on by external force.

mcqs.q: The value of acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface is approximately:
mcqs.explanation: g = 9.8 m/s² (approx).

mcqs.q: The unit of momentum is:
mcqs.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity; unit = kg·m/s.

mcqs.q: Which law explains rocket propulsion?
mcqs.explanation: Rocket propulsion: action (gas expelled) — reaction (rocket moves forward).

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a scalar quantity?
mcqs.explanation: Displacement has direction — vector; rest are scalar.

mcqs.q: The dimensional formula of force is:
mcqs.explanation: Force = mass × acceleration = M × LT⁻² = MLT⁻².

mcqs.q: Which law gives the relation between force and acceleration?
mcqs.explanation: F = ma (Newton's second law).

mcqs.q: The energy possessed by a body due to its motion is:
mcqs.explanation: KE = (1/2)mv².

mcqs.q: The rate of doing work is called:
mcqs.explanation: Power = Work/Time. SI unit: Watt.

mcqs.q: The acceleration due to gravity on Moon is approximately:
mcqs.explanation: Moon's gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's — 1.6 m/s².

mcqs.q: The speed of light in vacuum is approximately —
mcqs.explanation: Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum — the fastest speed possible in nature.

mcqs.q: Sound waves CANNOT travel through —
mcqs.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium; there are no particles in vacuum to vibrate.

mcqs.q: The audible frequency range for human beings is —
mcqs.explanation: Humans hear between 20 Hz and 20 kHz; below is infrasound (earthquakes) and above is ultrasound (SONAR).

mcqs.q: The splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours is called —
mcqs.explanation: Dispersion occurs because each colour has a different speed/refractive index in glass — violet bends most, red least.

mcqs.q: According to Ohm's law, the relation between potential difference (V), current (I) and resistance (R) is —
mcqs.explanation: Ohm's law states V = IR at constant temperature; resistance R = V/I.

mcqs.q: The Raman Effect is related to —
mcqs.explanation: C.V. Raman (1928) discovered the inelastic scattering of light by molecules, winning the 1930 Nobel Prize.

mcqs.q: The filament of an electric bulb is made of —
mcqs.explanation: Tungsten has a very high melting point (≈ 3,400°C) and high resistivity, ideal for a glowing filament.

mcqs.q: In the diagram, a ray parallel to the principal axis strikes a convex lens. After refraction it passes through:
mcqs.explanation: A parallel ray refracts through the principal focus F of a convex lens.

mcqs.q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
mcqs.explanation: Convex mirror — always erect, diminished image with a wider field of view.

mcqs.q: Sound waves CANNOT travel through:
mcqs.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium — it cannot travel in vacuum.

mcqs.q: In the circuit shown, using Ohm's law the current I is:
The SI unit of electric current is:
mcqs.explanation: Current is measured in ampere (A); volt = potential, ohm = resistance, watt = power.

mcqs.q: The speed of light in vacuum is approximately:
mcqs.explanation: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s (3,00,000 km per second).

mcqs.q: The loudness of a sound depends on its:
mcqs.explanation: Loudness ∝ amplitude²; pitch depends on frequency.

mcqs.q: A dentist uses a mirror that gives an erect and magnified image of a tooth placed close to it. The mirror is —
mcqs.explanation: A concave mirror forms a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is within its focus — ideal for a dentist or shaving mirror.

mcqs.q: An ammeter, the instrument that measures electric current, is always connected in the circuit in —
mcqs.explanation: The whole circuit current must pass through it, so the ammeter (low resistance) is joined in series; a voltmeter is joined in parallel.

mcqs.q: A pencil partly dipped in a glass of water appears bent at the water surface. This is due to —
mcqs.explanation: Light bends when passing between air and water because its speed changes — this bending is refraction.

mcqs.q: Bats fly safely in the dark because they navigate using —
mcqs.explanation: Bats emit high-frequency (above 20 kHz) ultrasonic pulses and judge obstacles or prey from the echoes — called echolocation.

mcqs.q: The blue colour of the clear sky is explained by which optical phenomenon?
mcqs.explanation: Shorter (blue) wavelengths of sunlight are scattered far more by air molecules than longer (red) ones, making the sky look blue.

mcqs.q: According to the first law of reflection, the angle of incidence is always —
options: Equal to the angle of reflection
Greater than the angle of reflection
Less than the angle of reflection
mcqs.explanation: For every reflection, angle of incidence = angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.

mcqs.q: The sparkling of a diamond, the mirage in a desert and the working of optical fibres are all based on —
mcqs.explanation: Light striking the boundary beyond the critical angle is totally reflected inside the denser medium — the principle of TIR.

mcqs.q: When white light passes through a prism, which colour bends (deviates) the most?
mcqs.explanation: Violet has the greatest refractive index in glass, so it deviates most; red deviates least (VIBGYOR order).

mcqs.q: To hear a distinct echo in air (at ~332 m/s), the minimum distance between the source and the reflecting surface should be about —
mcqs.explanation: The ear needs ≥0.1 s between the original and reflected sound; sound covers about 33 m in 0.1 s, so the reflector must be ≈17.2 m away.

mcqs.q: The commercial unit of electrical energy, one kilowatt-hour (1 kWh or "1 unit"), equals —
mcqs.explanation: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ joules — the "unit" shown on electricity bills.

mcqs.q: Domestic electric wiring is done in parallel rather than in series because in a parallel circuit —
options: Every appliance gets the same voltage and can be switched independently
Current in every branch is the same
mcqs.explanation: In parallel, each appliance receives the full supply voltage and works independently; in series, all devices share the voltage and fail together.

mcqs.q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
mcqs.explanation: Silver has the lowest resistivity of all metals; copper and aluminium are used instead only because silver is costly.

mcqs.q: Seismographs record low-frequency waves produced before and during earthquakes. Waves below 20 Hz are called —
mcqs.explanation: Frequencies below the 20 Hz lower limit of human hearing are infrasonic (elephants and whales also use them).

mcqs.q: A resistor of 4 Ω carries a current of 3 A. The potential difference across it is —
mcqs.explanation: Using Ohm's law V = I × R = 3 × 4 = 12 V.

mcqs.q: When an object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror, the image formed is —
options: Real, erect and of same size
mcqs.explanation: This is the shaving-mirror case: the concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged virtual image for objects inside the focus.

mcqs.q: Light travels fastest in:
mcqs.explanation: Speed of light is maximum in vacuum: about 3 × 10^8 m/s.

mcqs.q: One light-year is a unit of:
mcqs.explanation: A light-year measures distance — how far light travels in one year.

mcqs.q: Sound cannot travel through:
mcqs.explanation: Sound needs a material medium; there are no particles in vacuum.

mcqs.q: The audible range of sound for humans is:
mcqs.explanation: Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz; below is infrasound, above is ultrasound.

mcqs.q: A convex lens is used as a magnifying glass because when an object is close it forms a:
mcqs.explanation: Within the focal length, a convex lens acts as a simple magnifier.

mcqs.q: To correct myopia (short-sightedness), the lens used is:
mcqs.explanation: A concave (diverging) lens moves the image back onto the retina.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of electric resistance is:
mcqs.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).

mcqs.q: According to Ohm's law, V = IR, if current doubles with constant resistance, voltage:
mcqs.explanation: V is directly proportional to I at constant resistance.

mcqs.q: An electric fuse works on the:
mcqs.explanation: Excess current heats and melts the fuse wire, breaking the circuit.

mcqs.q: Which mirror is used as a vehicle rear-view mirror?
mcqs.explanation: A convex mirror gives a wide, erect field of view.

mcqs.q: The phenomenon responsible for a rainbow is:
mcqs.explanation: Raindrops split white light into its component colors (dispersion).

mcqs.q: Bats navigate in the dark using:
mcqs.explanation: Bats emit ultrasound and sense the reflected echoes (echolocation).

mcqs.q: SONAR works on the principle of:
mcqs.explanation: SONAR measures echo time of ultrasonic pulses to find ocean depths.

mcqs.q: The unit of electric power is:
mcqs.explanation: Power = energy per second, measured in watts (W).

mcqs.q: A split ring/commutator in an electric motor is used to:
options: reverse the current direction in the coil every half rotation
mcqs.explanation: Reversing current each half-turn keeps the torque in one direction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a good conductor of electricity?
mcqs.explanation: Metals like copper have free electrons — excellent conductors.

mcqs.q: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its:
mcqs.explanation: E = hν — photon energy grows with frequency.

mcqs.q: The blue color of the sky is due to:
options: scattering of shorter (blue) wavelengths of sunlight
mcqs.explanation: Air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths much more (Rayleigh scattering).

mcqs.q: Kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the commercial unit of:
mcqs.explanation: 1 kWh = 1 unit of electrical energy = 3.6 × 10^6 joules.

mcqs.q: A concave mirror is used in solar cookers because it:
options: converges parallel sunlight to a point (focus)
mcqs.explanation: Concave mirrors concentrate sunlight at the focus, producing heat.

mcqs.q: The electron was discovered by —
mcqs.explanation: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 through cathode-ray experiments.

mcqs.q: Atomic number of an element is equal to the number of —
mcqs.explanation: Atomic number Z = number of protons (also equal to electrons in a neutral atom); mass number A = protons + neutrons.

mcqs.q: Isotopes of an element have —
options: Same mass number, different atomic number
Same atomic number, different mass number
mcqs.explanation: Isotopes have identical protons (same Z) but different neutrons, so different mass numbers — e.g. ¹H, ²H, ³H.

mcqs.q: The 4th state of matter is —
mcqs.explanation: Plasma (ionised gas in the Sun, stars, neon signs) is the 4th state; BEC is the 5th.

mcqs.q: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating is which type of reaction?
mcqs.explanation: One reactant breaks into two products on heating — thermal decomposition used in lime kilns.

mcqs.q: The modern periodic table contains —
mcqs.explanation: The modern periodic table has 18 vertical groups and 7 horizontal periods, arranged by atomic number.

mcqs.q: Avogadro's number is —
mcqs.explanation: One mole of any substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles — the Avogadro constant.

mcqs.q: The chemical symbol of gold is:
mcqs.explanation: From Latin 'aurum' — Au. Ag is silver (argentum).

mcqs.q: The atomic number of carbon is 6. The number of protons in a carbon atom is:
mcqs.explanation: Atomic number = number of protons = 6 (mass number 12 = 6p + 6n).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a CHEMICAL change?
mcqs.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance (hydrated iron oxide) — a chemical change; the others are physical.

mcqs.q: The law of conservation of mass was given by:
mcqs.explanation: Lavoisier: mass of reactants = mass of products. Proust gave constant proportions.

mcqs.q: The valency of oxygen is:
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen needs 2 electrons to complete its octet → valency 2 (H₂O, CO₂).

mcqs.q: Camphor and naphthalene balls change directly from solid to gas. This process is:
mcqs.explanation: Sublimation — solid → gas directly (camphor, naphthalene, iodine, dry ice).

mcqs.q: The mass number (A) of an atom is equal to —
mcqs.explanation: Mass number A = protons + neutrons (nucleons); atomic number Z counts only the protons.

mcqs.q: Which of the following substances changes directly from solid to gas on heating (sublimation)?
mcqs.explanation: Camphor, naphthalene, iodine, dry ice and ammonium chloride sublime — they vaporise without melting.

mcqs.q: Dew drops seen on morning grass are an example of —
mcqs.explanation: Water vapour in air cools and turns into liquid droplets — a gas-to-liquid change called condensation.

mcqs.q: Elements of Group 18 of the modern periodic table (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) are called noble gases because they —
mcqs.explanation: Their outermost electron shells are completely filled, so they hardly form compounds and are chemically inert.

mcqs.q: Canal rays, which led to the discovery of the proton, were observed by —
mcqs.explanation: E. Goldstein's canal (anode) rays revealed the positively charged proton; Thomson discovered the electron, Chadwick the neutron.

mcqs.q: The dense positive centre of the atom, the nucleus, was discovered through the alpha-particle scattering (gold foil) experiment by —
mcqs.explanation: Rutherford (1911) concluded from alpha-particle deflections that nearly all mass and positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus.

mcqs.q: Isobars are atoms of different elements that have —
options: Same mass number, different atomic number
Same atomic number, different mass number
mcqs.explanation: Isobars share the mass number A but differ in protons Z — e.g. ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca; isotopes share Z instead.

mcqs.q: The fifth state of matter, obtained by cooling atoms to near absolute zero (−273°C), is —
mcqs.explanation: At near absolute zero, atoms merge into a single quantum state forming the Bose-Einstein Condensate; plasma is the 4th state.

mcqs.q: After oxygen, the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust is —
mcqs.explanation: The crust order is Oxygen (~46%) > Silicon (~28%) > Aluminium (~8%) > Iron (~5%) — remember O > Si > Al > Fe.

mcqs.q: The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing —
mcqs.explanation: Henry Moseley's modern periodic law orders elements by atomic number Z, fixing the anomalies of Mendeleev's mass-based table.

mcqs.q: Coating iron or steel articles with a thin layer of zinc to prevent rusting is called —
mcqs.explanation: In galvanisation, zinc acts as a protective sacrificial layer so air and moisture cannot reach and oxidise the iron.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an exothermic reaction?
mcqs.explanation: Slaking of quicklime releases a lot of heat; photosynthesis, CaCO₃ decomposition and electrolysis absorb energy.

mcqs.q: Which isotope is used in radiocarbon dating to determine the age of ancient wood and fossils? (हिंदी: रेडियोकार्बन डेटिंग में किस समस्थानिक का प्रयोग होता है?)
mcqs.explanation: Radioactive carbon-14 decays at a known rate after an organism dies, so its remaining fraction gives the sample's age.

mcqs.q: A chemical equation must be balanced because a balanced equation always obeys the —
mcqs.explanation: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so every element must have equal atoms on both sides — conservation of mass.

mcqs.q: The atomic number of an element equals the number of:
mcqs.explanation: Atomic number = number of protons in the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The molecular mass of water (H2O) is about:
Avogadro's number is approximately:
mcqs.explanation: One mole contains 6.022 × 10^23 particles.

mcqs.q: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called:
mcqs.explanation: Isotopes share proton count but differ in neutrons (e.g., C-12 and C-14).

mcqs.q: A pH of 7 indicates a solution that is:
mcqs.explanation: pH 7 (like pure water) is neutral; below acidic, above basic.

mcqs.q: The chemical formula of quicklime is:
mcqs.explanation: Quicklime is calcium oxide, CaO (slaked lime is Ca(OH)2).

mcqs.q: Rusting of iron requires:
mcqs.explanation: Iron rusts when both air (oxygen) and moisture are present.

mcqs.q: Sublimation is the change of state from:
mcqs.explanation: Camphor and naphthalene turn from solid directly to vapour — sublimation.

mcqs.q: Which gas is popularly known as 'laughing gas'?
mcqs.explanation: N2O (nitrous oxide) produces euphoria — laughing gas.

mcqs.q: The valency of carbon is:
mcqs.explanation: Carbon has 4 valence electrons → valency 4 (tetravalent).

mcqs.q: Which one is a compound?
mcqs.explanation: Water is chemically combined H and O in fixed ratio — a compound; brass is a mixture.

mcqs.q: The number of electrons in the outermost shell of noble gases (except helium) is:
mcqs.explanation: Full octet (8 electrons) makes noble gases inert.

mcqs.q: Balancing a chemical equation is done to satisfy the law of:
mcqs.explanation: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed — mass is conserved.

mcqs.q: Which is the lightest element?
mcqs.explanation: Hydrogen (atomic number 1) is the lightest element.

mcqs.q: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, hydrogen acts as:
mcqs.explanation: Hydrogen gains oxygen (is oxidized) and removes oxygen from view of O2 — it reduces oxygen; hence a reducing agent here.

mcqs.q: The gas used in electric bulbs to prevent oxidation of the filament is:
mcqs.explanation: Insert gases like argon or nitrogen are chemically inert at high temperature.

mcqs.q: Mole is the SI unit for:
mcqs.explanation: The mole measures amount of substance (6.022 × 10^23 units).

mcqs.q: Which separation technique is used to obtain salt from seawater?
mcqs.explanation: Seawater is left to evaporate, leaving salt crystals behind.

mcqs.q: A solution with pH 3 is:
mcqs.explanation: pH below 7 → acidic; 3 is strongly acidic.

mcqs.q: The chemical name of baking soda is:
mcqs.explanation: Baking soda = NaHCO3, sodium bicarbonate.

mcqs.q: Isobars are atoms with:
options: same mass number, different atomic numbers
mcqs.explanation: Isobars share mass number A but differ in proton number Z.

mcqs.q: Which one is a chemical change?
mcqs.explanation: Burning forms new substances (CO2, ash) — a chemical change.

mcqs.q: The number of moles in 44 g of CO2 is:
mcqs.explanation: Molar mass of CO2 = 44 g/mol → 44 g = 1 mole.

mcqs.q: Cathode rays are actually streams of:
mcqs.explanation: J.J. Thomson showed cathode rays are negatively charged electrons.

mcqs.q: Which gas makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere?
mcqs.explanation: Nitrogen dominates the atmosphere at about 78% by volume.

mcqs.q: A neutral solution has a pH of —
mcqs.explanation: pH 7 (pure water) is neutral; below 7 acidic and above 7 basic.

mcqs.q: Milk of magnesia, used as an antacid, is chemically —
mcqs.explanation: Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)₂ is a mild base that neutralises excess stomach HCl.

mcqs.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
mcqs.explanation: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature; gallium melts at ~29.8°C (slightly above room temperature).

mcqs.q: The most abundant metal in the Earth's crust is —
mcqs.explanation: Aluminium (~8%) is the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element in the crust after oxygen and silicon.

mcqs.q: The acid present in an ant sting is —
mcqs.explanation: Ants inject formic acid; rubbing baking soda neutralises it.

mcqs.q: Bleaching powder is chemically known as —
mcqs.explanation: Bleaching powder is CaOCl₂ (calcium oxychloride), used as a disinfectant and bleaching agent.

mcqs.q: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with —
mcqs.explanation: Stainless steel = iron + chromium (+ nickel + carbon); chromium forms a protective oxide layer preventing rust.

mcqs.q: The pH of a neutral solution is:
mcqs.explanation: pH < 7 acidic, pH = 7 neutral (pure water), pH > 7 basic.

mcqs.q: Blue litmus paper turns red in:
mcqs.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: The metal which is liquid at room temperature is:
mcqs.explanation: Mercury (Hg) — used in thermometers; the only liquid metal.

mcqs.q: The most abundant metal in the Earth's crust is:
mcqs.explanation: Aluminium is the most abundant metal (oxygen is the most abundant element).

mcqs.q: Brass is an alloy of:
mcqs.explanation: Brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin.

mcqs.q: Rusting of iron is prevented by coating it with zinc. This process is called:
mcqs.explanation: Galvanisation — zinc coating protects iron from rust.

mcqs.q: Blue litmus paper turns ______ in an acid.
mcqs.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: Common salt is chemically:
mcqs.explanation: Table salt = NaCl (sodium chloride).

mcqs.q: Sodium is stored under kerosene because it:
options: reacts violently with air and water moisture
mcqs.explanation: Sodium ignites on contact with moisture; kerosene prevents exposure.

mcqs.q: The pH of lemon juice is approximately:
mcqs.explanation: Citric acid makes lemon juice strongly acidic (pH ≈ 2-3).

mcqs.q: Which acid is present in the human stomach?
mcqs.explanation: Gastric juice contains HCl which aids digestion.

mcqs.q: Ammonia solution turns red litmus:
mcqs.explanation: Ammonia is a base; bases turn red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: The purity of gold is measured in:
mcqs.explanation: 24-carat is pure gold; 22-carat alloyed with copper/silver for ornaments.

mcqs.q: Washing soda's chemical formula is:
mcqs.explanation: Washing soda is hydrated sodium carbonate (Na2CO3·10H2O).

mcqs.q: Galvanization is coating iron with:
mcqs.explanation: Zinc coating prevents rusting of iron sheets/pipes.

mcqs.q: Bleaching powder is produced by the action of chlorine on:
mcqs.explanation: Cl2 + Ca(OH)2 → bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl.

mcqs.q: An antacid like milk of magnesia works because it is:
mcqs.explanation: Mg(OH)2 is a mild base that neutralizes HCl.

mcqs.q: Aqua regia, which can dissolve gold, is a mixture of:
mcqs.explanation: Concentrated HCl : HNO3 in 3:1 ratio forms aqua regia ('royal water').

mcqs.q: The cell was discovered by —
mcqs.explanation: Robert Hooke saw dead cork cells in 1665 and coined the term "cell"; Leeuwenhoek first saw living (micro)organisms.

mcqs.q: The powerhouse of the cell is —
mcqs.explanation: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration and release energy stored as ATP.

mcqs.q: The number of bones in an adult human body is —
mcqs.explanation: An adult has 206 bones; a newborn has about 300, which fuse during growth.

mcqs.q: Which blood group person can donate blood to all groups (universal donor)?
mcqs.explanation: Group O (especially O negative) has no A/B antigens on RBCs, so it can be donated to everyone.

mcqs.q: The average lifespan of human Red Blood Cells is —
mcqs.explanation: RBCs survive about 120 days and are then destroyed in the spleen (the graveyard of RBCs).

mcqs.q: The stapes, the smallest bone of the human body, is located in the —
mcqs.explanation: Stapes lies in the middle ear and transmits sound vibrations to the inner ear; it is barely 2–3 mm long.

mcqs.q: Which organelle is called the "suicidal bag" of the cell?
mcqs.explanation: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that can even digest the cell itself on rupture — hence suicidal bag.

mcqs.q: Which organelle is called the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
mcqs.explanation: Mitochondria release energy as ATP during respiration.

mcqs.q: In the heart diagram, the chamber marked ★ (thick-walled, pumps blood to the whole body) is the:
mcqs.explanation: The left ventricle drives oxygenated blood through the aorta to the entire body — hence the thickest wall.

mcqs.q: The largest organ of the human body is:
mcqs.explanation: Skin is the largest organ; the liver is the largest internal organ/gland.

mcqs.q: Oxygen is transported in blood by:
mcqs.explanation: Haemoglobin, the red pigment of RBC, binds oxygen.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
mcqs.explanation: Scurvy — bleeding gums; citrus fruits prevent it. D→rickets, A→night blindness, B1→beriberi.

mcqs.q: The universal blood donor group is:
mcqs.explanation: O− has no A, B or Rh antigens — universal donor; AB+ is the universal recipient.

mcqs.q: The 'powerhouse of the cell' is the:
mcqs.explanation: Mitochondria produce ATP — the cell's energy currency.

mcqs.q: The cell was discovered by:
mcqs.explanation: Robert Hooke saw 'cells' in cork under his microscope in 1665.

mcqs.q: The largest organ of the human body is the:
mcqs.explanation: Skin is the largest organ; liver is the largest internal gland/organ by mass debates — standard answer: skin.

mcqs.q: Which blood cells help fight infection?
options: Plasma cells are not blood cells
mcqs.explanation: White blood cells (leukocytes) defend the body against pathogens.

mcqs.q: The human heart has how many chambers?
mcqs.explanation: Two atria + two ventricles = 4 chambers.

mcqs.q: Insulin, which controls blood sugar, is secreted by the:
mcqs.explanation: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets produce insulin.

mcqs.q: The largest bone in the human body is the:
mcqs.explanation: The thigh bone (femur) is longest and strongest; stapes is smallest.

mcqs.q: Hemoglobin in blood contains which metal?
mcqs.explanation: Iron in heme binds oxygen, giving blood its red color.

mcqs.q: The control centre of the cell containing DNA is the:
mcqs.explanation: The nucleus stores genetic material and directs activities.

mcqs.q: Normal human body temperature is about:
mcqs.explanation: Average is 37°C (98.6°F).

mcqs.q: Which vitamin is produced in the skin using sunlight?
mcqs.explanation: UV-B converts skin sterols into vitamin D ('sunshine vitamin').

mcqs.q: The smallest bone in the human body is located in the:
mcqs.explanation: Stapes, in the middle ear, is the smallest bone.

mcqs.q: Plants absorb water from soil mainly through:
mcqs.explanation: Root hairs massively increase absorptive surface.

mcqs.q: Which pigment carries oxygen in blood?
mcqs.explanation: Hemoglobin (iron-based) transports oxygen; chlorophyll is plant pigment.

mcqs.q: During photosynthesis, plants release —
mcqs.explanation: Water molecules are split during photosynthesis and oxygen is released as a by-product.

mcqs.q: Xylem in plants transports —
mcqs.explanation: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to leaves; phloem carries food.

mcqs.q: Scurvy is caused by the deficiency of —
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency causes scurvy — bleeding gums and weakness; amla and citrus fruits prevent it.

mcqs.q: Rickets in children is caused by the deficiency of —
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin D (calciferol) deficiency weakens bones causing rickets; sunlight is the natural source.

mcqs.q: Malaria is spread by the bite of —
mcqs.explanation: The female Anopheles mosquito transmits the Plasmodium protozoan that causes malaria.

mcqs.q: BCG vaccine provides protection against —
mcqs.explanation: Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) is given at birth to protect against tuberculosis.

mcqs.q: Which vitamin contains the metal cobalt in its structure?
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin) contains cobalt at the centre of its ring structure.

mcqs.q: In the photosynthesis diagram, gas X released by the leaf is:
mcqs.explanation: Photosynthesis releases oxygen and stores energy as glucose.

mcqs.q: The green pigment in leaves that traps sunlight is:
mcqs.explanation: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light energy.

mcqs.q: Loss of water vapour from leaves occurs mainly through:
mcqs.explanation: Stomata — tiny pores on the leaf surface, guarded by guard cells.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of iodine in the diet causes:
mcqs.explanation: Goitre — swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck.

mcqs.q: Malaria is spread by the bite of:
mcqs.explanation: Female Anopheles mosquito transmits the Plasmodium protozoan (Aedes spreads dengue).

mcqs.q: BCG vaccine provides protection against:
mcqs.explanation: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) — against tuberculosis.

mcqs.q: Which component of food is the MAIN source of energy?
mcqs.explanation: Carbohydrates (rice, wheat) are the chief energy providers; proteins build the body.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis mainly requires:
options: sunlight, water, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll
mcqs.explanation: CO2 + H2O + light → glucose + O2 in chlorophyll-containing chloroplasts.

mcqs.q: The green pigment in leaves is:
mcqs.explanation: Chlorophyll captures light energy for photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Malaria is transmitted by the bite of:
mcqs.explanation: Female Anopheles spreads Plasmodium (malaria parasite).

mcqs.q: Dengue is spread mainly by:
mcqs.explanation: Aedes aegypti transmits the dengue virus (day-biting).

mcqs.q: Which disease is caused by bacteria?
mcqs.explanation: TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis; cold/AIDS are viral, dengue viral.

mcqs.q: Roughage (dietary fibre) helps mainly in:
mcqs.explanation: Fibre adds bulk and prevents constipation.

mcqs.q: Proteins are made of:
mcqs.explanation: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.

mcqs.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness?
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin A (retinol) deficiency impairs vision in dim light.

mcqs.q: The primary site of photosynthesis in a leaf cell is the:
mcqs.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and host the light reactions.

mcqs.q: Goitre can be prevented by using:
mcqs.explanation: Iodized salt supplies dietary iodine for the thyroid.

mcqs.q: Stomata in leaves function to:
options: exchange gases and lose water vapour
mcqs.explanation: Guard cells open/close stomata for CO2 intake and transpiration.

mcqs.q: Kwashiorkor is caused mainly by deficiency of:
mcqs.explanation: Severe protein malnutrition in children → kwashiorkor.

mcqs.q: Pasteurization of milk involves:
options: heating to kill harmful microbes then rapid cooling
mcqs.explanation: Named after Louis Pasteur; typical 72°C for 15 s then chilling.

mcqs.q: How many major organ systems are present in the human body?
mcqs.explanation: Standard biology counts 11 organ systems, from the integumentary (skin) to the reproductive system.

mcqs.q: The largest gland of the human body is —
mcqs.explanation: Liver (~1.5 kg) is the largest gland and largest internal organ; it secretes bile.

mcqs.q: Which node acts as the pacemaker of the heart?
mcqs.explanation: The sino-atrial (SA) node in the right atrium initiates each heartbeat and sets the rhythm (~72/min).

mcqs.q: The kidneys are part of which organ system?
mcqs.explanation: Kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra form the urinary system that removes urea as urine.

mcqs.q: Insulin, which lowers blood sugar, is secreted by the —
mcqs.explanation: Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas secrete insulin; its shortage causes diabetes mellitus.

mcqs.q: Most absorption of digested food takes place in the —
mcqs.explanation: The long, villi-lined small intestine absorbs over 90% of nutrients; the large intestine mainly absorbs water.

mcqs.q: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing?
mcqs.explanation: The medulla oblongata regulates involuntary vital functions — heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure; cerebellum handles balance.

mcqs.q: How many bones are there in the adult human skeleton? (हिंदी: वयस्क मानव शरीर में कितनी अस्थियाँ होती हैं?)
mcqs.explanation: An adult has 206 bones; a newborn has about 300 soft bones that gradually fuse during growth.

mcqs.q: The longest bone in the human body is the —
mcqs.explanation: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone, joining the hip to the knee.

mcqs.q: The smallest bone of the human body, the stapes, is located in the —
mcqs.explanation: The stirrup-shaped stapes (about 3 mm) lies in the middle ear and transmits sound vibrations to the inner ear.

mcqs.q: Which is the largest organ of the human body?
mcqs.explanation: Skin (about 1.5–2 m²) is the largest organ of the body; the liver is only the largest internal organ/gland.

mcqs.q: In sunlight, the human skin helps synthesise which vitamin?
mcqs.explanation: UV rays acting on a cholesterol derivative in the skin produce vitamin D, which helps absorb calcium.

mcqs.q: Blood cells (RBCs, WBCs and platelets) are produced in the —
mcqs.explanation: Red bone marrow inside certain bones manufactures all three types of blood cells throughout life.

mcqs.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
mcqs.explanation: Two atria plus two ventricles make 4 chambers, keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood fully separated.

mcqs.q: Exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs takes place through the —
mcqs.explanation: About 300 million thin-walled alveoli provide the huge surface where O₂ enters the blood and CO₂ leaves it.

mcqs.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the —
mcqs.explanation: Each kidney contains about 1 million nephrons, the tiny filters that remove urea from blood; the neuron is the unit of the nervous system.

mcqs.q: Goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland, is caused by the deficiency of —
mcqs.explanation: Iodine is essential for making thyroxine; its deficiency forces the thyroid to swell, producing goitre.

mcqs.q: Which hormone, called the "emergency" or fight-or-flight hormone, is released in times of stress?
mcqs.explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands increases heartbeat, breathing rate and blood sugar to prepare the body for emergencies.

mcqs.q: Which part of the brain maintains balance and muscular coordination?
mcqs.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscles for balance and posture; the medulla controls involuntary vitals like heartbeat.

mcqs.q: The enzyme present in saliva that digests starch is —
mcqs.explanation: Salivary amylase breaks starch into maltose in the mouth; pepsin digests proteins in the stomach.

mcqs.q: Cardiac muscle, found only in the walls of the heart, is —
mcqs.explanation: Cardiac muscle is involuntary but striated and branched — it keeps contracting rhythmically without conscious control.

mcqs.q: Which blood cells primarily defend the body against infection?
mcqs.explanation: WBCs (leucocytes) engulf germs and build immunity; platelets help in clotting and RBCs carry oxygen.

mcqs.q: The pulmonary artery is unusual among arteries because it carries —
mcqs.explanation: All other arteries carry oxygen-rich blood, but the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.

mcqs.q: The largest artery of the human body is the —
mcqs.explanation: The aorta arises from the left ventricle and distributes oxygenated blood to the entire body; the vena cava is the largest vein.

mcqs.q: Urea is synthesised in the human body mainly in the —
mcqs.explanation: The liver converts toxic ammonia into urea; the kidney only filters the urea out through urine.

mcqs.q: A patient whose kidneys have failed is treated with a machine that filters wastes from the blood. This process is called —
mcqs.explanation: In haemodialysis an artificial filter removes urea and excess salts when the nephrons can no longer do so.

mcqs.q: Which part of the brain is the seat of thinking, memory and intelligence?
mcqs.explanation: The large, folded cerebrum handles conscious thought, learning, memory and decision-making.

mcqs.q: Reflex actions such as the knee-jerk are controlled by the —
mcqs.explanation: Spinal reflexes are processed by the spinal cord without involving the brain, which makes the response much faster.

mcqs.q: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the —
mcqs.explanation: The neuron (nerve cell) with its dendrites, cell body and axon carries electrical impulses throughout the body.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of growth hormone from the pituitary gland in childhood results in —
mcqs.explanation: Too little growth hormone causes dwarfism, while its excess in childhood causes gigantism.

mcqs.q: The male sex hormone testosterone is secreted by the —
mcqs.explanation: The testes secrete testosterone, which develops and maintains male secondary sexual characters.

mcqs.q: Bile, which helps in the digestion of fats, is produced by the liver and stored in the —
mcqs.explanation: The gall bladder stores and concentrates bile before releasing it into the small intestine through the bile duct.

mcqs.q: A person with blood group O negative is called a universal donor because —
options: Their red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens
They can receive blood from any group
mcqs.explanation: O− red cells have no A, B or Rh antigens, so no recipient's antibodies attack them; AB+ persons are universal recipients.

mcqs.q: The metal present in haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying pigment of blood, is —
mcqs.explanation: Iron in the haem part of haemoglobin binds oxygen; iron deficiency reduces this capacity and causes anaemia.

mcqs.q: How many chromosomes are present in a normal human body (somatic) cell? (हिंदी: मानव दैहिक कोशिका में कितने गुणसूत्र होते हैं?)
mcqs.explanation: Somatic cells carry 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes; gametes (sperm/ovum) carry only half, i.e. 23.

mcqs.q: In humans, fertilisation of the ovum by the sperm normally occurs in the —
mcqs.explanation: Sperm meets the ovum in the fallopian tube (oviduct); the resulting zygote then implants in the uterus.

mcqs.q: The junction between two neurons across which a chemical messenger passes the nerve impulse is called a —
mcqs.explanation: At the synapse, neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine carry the signal from one neuron to the next.

mcqs.q: The laboratory thermometer in the diagram shows the mercury level. What temperature is it reading?
mcqs.explanation: The mercury top sits exactly on the 37°C mark on the scale (each small step between labels is 1°C).

mcqs.q: The water-cycle diagram labels an arrow X rising from the sea towards the cloud. Process X is
mcqs.explanation: Water vapour rising from the sea surface into the air is evaporation (driven by the sun’s heat).

mcqs.explanation: When condensed water droplets in clouds become heavy and fall as rain, the process is precipitation.

mcqs.q: The food-chain diagram shows Grass → Deer → Lion. The Lion occupies which trophic level?
mcqs.explanation: Grass produces, the deer eats grass (primary consumer), and the lion eating the deer is the secondary (top) consumer.

mcqs.explanation: A herbivore feeding directly on producers (grass) is a primary consumer.

mcqs.q: In the leaf diagram, the broad green part labeled A (lamina) is mainly where
options: The plant breathes in soil air
mcqs.explanation: The lamina contains chlorophyll-rich mesophyll cells — the main site of photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows a compass placed near the North pole of a bar magnet. Which pole of the compass NEEDLE will point towards the magnet’s N pole?
mcqs.explanation: Unlike poles attract: the compass needle’s SOUTH pole turns toward the magnet’s North pole.

mcqs.q: Why does a vaccinated person usually recover from infection faster than an unvaccinated one?
options: The vaccine kills the pathogen directly on entry
Memory B-cells and T-cells mount a faster, larger secondary immune response
The pathogen becomes weaker every year
mcqs.explanation: The passage explains that memory cells 'recognise it instantly and mount a faster, larger and more targeted secondary response' — this speed is the vaccinated person's advantage.
mcqs.passage:
Passage — How Vaccines Train the Body

A vaccine is a rehearsal for an invasion. By introducing the immune system to a harmless form of a pathogen — an inactivated virus, a protein fragment, or instructions for building a single viral protein — it lets the body build defences before a real attack. The first exposure produces primary immune responses: antibodies rise slowly, and memory B-cells and T-cells take up long-term residence in the body. When the genuine pathogen arrives, these memory cells recognise it instantly and mount a faster, larger and more targeted secondary response, which is why a vaccinated person may fall only mildly ill, or not at all. Boosters exploit the same logic: each additional dose re-stimulates memory cells and broadens the antibody pool, raising protection back to its peak. Protection also travels beyond the individual. When a large enough share of a population is immune, the pathogen can no longer find reliable chains of transmission — the community-level shield called herd immunity. It is this principle, applied across two centuries, that rid the world of smallpox by 1980 and has pushed polio to the edge of extinction.

mcqs.q: The purpose of a booster dose is to —
options: replace the immune system with new cells
re-stimulate memory cells and raise protection back to its peak
treat an ongoing infection with antibodies
change the person's DNA to fight disease
mcqs.explanation: 'Each additional dose re-stimulates memory cells and broadens the antibody pool, raising protection back to its peak' — that is the booster's role.

mcqs.q: Why have solar and wind become cheap, according to the passage?
options: Governments give unlimited free land for farms
Economies of scale and better engineering cut costs as production doubled
Sunlight and wind have become stronger over the years
mcqs.explanation: 'The reason is manufacturing, not miracle — each doubling of production has steadily cut the cost... through economies of scale and better engineering.'
mcqs.passage:
Passage — The Promise and Puzzle of Renewable Power

Solar panels and wind turbines have moved from novelty to necessity: in many countries, a new solar farm now produces electricity more cheaply than a new coal plant. The reason is manufacturing, not miracle — each doubling of production has steadily cut the cost of panels and turbines through economies of scale and better engineering. Yet renewables carry a puzzle that coal never posed. The sun sets; the wind stalls. This intermittency means generation does not automatically match demand, which arrives in its own stubborn rhythm of mornings and evenings. The emerging answers are three: storage, with falling-cost batteries banking noon's surplus for the evening peak; geography, since power flows through grids from windy or sunny regions to distant consumers; and flexibility, in which industries and chargers adjust their demand to when supply is abundant. No single fix is sufficient — but together they sketch a grid that is cleaner, more distributed and, its engineers argue, more resilient than the centralised model of the coal age.

mcqs.q: The 'puzzle that coal never posed' refers to —
options: the intermittency of solar and wind, so generation does not automatically match demand
solar panels being difficult to clean
mcqs.explanation: Coal burns on demand, but 'the sun sets; the wind stalls' — renewables are intermittent, so supply does not follow the rhythm of demand.

mcqs.explanation: The passage lists storage, geography (grids) and flexibility as the three answers; taller chimneys are a feature of thermal plants, not a renewable-integration fix.

mcqs.q: The Constitution of India came into force on —
mcqs.explanation: Adopted on 26 November 1949, the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950 — under Article 394 key provisions (citizenship, elections) took effect from 26 November 1949 itself.

mcqs.q: The Objectives Resolution, which became the basis of the Preamble, was moved by —
mcqs.explanation: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946; adopted on 22 January 1947, it became the basis of the Preamble that precedes Article 1.

mcqs.q: The Preamble was amended for the first and only time by —
mcqs.explanation: Using the Article 368 amendment power, the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity into the Preamble.

mcqs.q: Which case held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution?
mcqs.explanation: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Berubari (1960) and held the Preamble is part of the Constitution — the Article 368 amendment power cannot destroy its basic structure.

mcqs.q: The idea of the words "Justice — social, economic, political" in the Preamble is drawn from —
mcqs.explanation: Justice (social, economic, political) traces to the Russian Revolution; Liberty, Equality, Fraternity to the French Revolution — all embedded in the Preamble preceding Article 1.

mcqs.q: How many members signed the Constitution of India?
mcqs.explanation: Of the 299 members after Partition, 284 signed on 24 January 1950; under Article 394, certain provisions came into force the same adoption day (26 November 1949).

mcqs.q: Who was the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly?
mcqs.explanation: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946; Sinha only chaired the first meeting — the Assembly served as the provisional legislature until the Article 79 Parliament began.

mcqs.q: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constitution?
mcqs.explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was Chairman of the Drafting Committee formed on 29 August 1947.

mcqs.q: The Constitution of India came into effect on:
mcqs.explanation: Constitution adopted on 26 Nov 1949 but came into effect on 26 January 1950 — Republic Day.

mcqs.q: The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added to the Preamble by:
mcqs.explanation: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 (Mini-Constitution) added these three words to the Preamble.

mcqs.q: How many members were there in the Constituent Assembly when the Constitution was finally adopted?
mcqs.explanation: After partition, the Assembly had 299 members (down from 389 originally).

mcqs.q: The idea of the Constitution of India was first given by:
mcqs.explanation: M.N. Roy in 1934 first proposed the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India.

mcqs.q: Who was the first temporary President of the Constituent Assembly?
mcqs.explanation: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha presided over the first meeting on 9 Dec 1946; Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 Dec 1946.

mcqs.q: The Constitution of India is the longest written constitution in the world. How many articles did it originally have?
mcqs.explanation: Originally 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules. Now it has ~470 articles, 25 parts, 12 schedules.

mcqs.q: From which country did India borrow the idea of Fundamental Rights?
mcqs.explanation: Fundamental Rights (Part III) borrowed from the US Bill of Rights.

mcqs.q: From which country did India borrow the Directive Principles of State Policy?
mcqs.explanation: DPSP (Part IV) borrowed from the Irish Constitution.

mcqs.q: The Preamble of the Constitution guarantees all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explanation: Property is not in the Preamble; it was a Fundamental Right (Article 31) but removed by 44th Amendment (1978) and made a legal right under Article 300A.

mcqs.q: The total time taken to frame the Constitution was:
mcqs.explanation: The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months, 18 days to frame the Constitution.

mcqs.q: 'Constitution Day' (Samvidhan Diwas) is celebrated on:
mcqs.explanation: Constitution Day is celebrated on 26 November (date of adoption in 1949), declared in 2015.

mcqs.q: The Indian Constitution is a combination of:
mcqs.explanation: Indian Constitution is federal in form but unitary in spirit (quasi-federal) — Dr. Ambedkar.

mcqs.q: Who is known as the 'Father of the Indian Constitution'?
mcqs.explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee, is known as the Father of the Indian Constitution.

mcqs.q: How many schedules did the original Constitution have?
mcqs.explanation: Originally 8 schedules. The 9th was added by 1st Amendment (1951); today there are 12.

mcqs.q: Which Articles of the Constitution deal with the Right to Equality?
mcqs.explanation: The Right to Equality spans Articles 14 to 18 — equality before law, non-discrimination, equal opportunity, abolition of untouchability and titles.

mcqs.q: The Right to Education is guaranteed under which Article?
mcqs.explanation: Article 21A (inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002) makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6-14 years.

mcqs.q: Which writ is issued to release a person from unlawful detention?
mcqs.explanation: Habeas Corpus literally means "to have the body" — it orders the authority to produce the detainee before the court. It flows from Article 32/226.

mcqs.q: The Right against Exploitation is contained in —
mcqs.explanation: Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and begar; Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories and mines.

mcqs.q: Prohibition of employment of children below 14 years in mines is under —
mcqs.explanation: Article 24 of Part III forbids employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or hazardous work.

mcqs.q: Which Article protects a person from self-incrimination?
mcqs.explanation: Article 20(3) provides protection against self-incrimination; 20(1) bans ex-post-facto laws, 20(2) bans double jeopardy.

mcqs.q: High Courts can issue writs under which Article?
mcqs.explanation: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for FRs as well as "any other purpose" — wider than the Supreme Court's Article 32.

mcqs.q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the Right to Equality?
mcqs.explanation: Articles 14-18 deal with the Right to Equality (Art 14: equality before law, Art 15: prohibition of discrimination, Art 16: equality in employment, Art 17: abolition of untouchability, Art 18: abolition of titles).

mcqs.q: The 'Right to Constitutional Remedies' is provided under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 32 — called by Dr. Ambedkar the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution — gives citizens the right to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

mcqs.q: Which Article abolishes untouchability?
mcqs.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form — enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability is an offence punishable by law.

mcqs.q: The Right to Property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by which Amendment?
mcqs.explanation: The 44th Amendment Act (1978) removed the Right to Property (Art 31) from Fundamental Rights and made it a legal/constitutional right under Article 300A.

mcqs.q: How many Fundamental Rights does the Indian Constitution currently guarantee?
mcqs.explanation: Originally 7; now 6 after removal of Right to Property (44th Amendment, 1978).

mcqs.q: The writ 'Habeas Corpus' literally means:
mcqs.explanation: Habeas Corpus = 'You may have the body' — issued against illegal detention, ordering the authority to produce the detainee.

mcqs.q: The Right against Exploitation is provided under Articles:
mcqs.explanation: Article 23 prohibits trafficking and forced labour (begar); Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories/mines.

mcqs.q: How many writs can be issued under Article 32?
mcqs.explanation: Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.

mcqs.q: The Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression is under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees Freedom of Speech and Expression; subject to reasonable restrictions under 19(2).

mcqs.q: Right to Education was made a Fundamental Right by which Amendment?
mcqs.explanation: The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 21A — Right to Education for children aged 6-14 years as a Fundamental Right.

mcqs.q: Which Article prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth?
mcqs.explanation: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.

mcqs.q: The 'Mandamus' writ is issued to:
options: Compel a public authority to perform its duty
Quash an order of lower court
Inquire into legality of a public office
mcqs.explanation: Mandamus = 'We command' — issued to compel a public authority to perform its statutory duty.

mcqs.q: The Right to Education is under which Article?
mcqs.explanation: 21A added by 86th Amendment (2002).

mcqs.q: Article 17 abolishes:
mcqs.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability.

mcqs.q: Right to Freedom of Religion is in Articles:
mcqs.explanation: Articles 25-28 = Freedom of Religion.

mcqs.q: The six fundamental freedoms are under Article:
mcqs.explanation: Article 19 has six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession).

mcqs.q: Protection against arrest is under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 22 — protection against arrest and detention.

mcqs.q: The Right to Equality is in Articles:
mcqs.explanation: Articles 14-18 = Right to Equality.

mcqs.q: Article 14 provides:
mcqs.explanation: Article 14 — Equality before law & equal protection of laws.

mcqs.q: Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in:
mcqs.explanation: Article 16 — equality in public employment.

mcqs.q: Article 20 provides protection against:
options: Ex post facto laws and double jeopardy
mcqs.explanation: Article 20 — no ex post facto laws, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination.

mcqs.q: Article 23 prohibits:
options: Traffic in human beings and forced labour
mcqs.explanation: Article 23 — prohibits trafficking and forced labour (begar).

mcqs.q: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below ___ in factories/mines:
mcqs.explanation: Article 24 — no child below 14 in factories, mines, or hazardous work.

mcqs.q: Article 25 provides:
mcqs.explanation: Article 25 — Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, propagation of religion.

mcqs.q: Right of minorities to establish educational institutions is under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 30 — Right of minorities to establish educational institutions.

mcqs.q: Which writ is called 'bulwark of personal liberty'?
mcqs.explanation: Habeas Corpus — bulwark of personal liberty against illegal detention.

mcqs.q: Number of Fundamental Rights after 44th Amendment:
mcqs.explanation: Originally 7; after removal of Right to Property — 6.

mcqs.q: Fundamental Rights are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
mcqs.explanation: Part III (Articles 12-35) contains the Fundamental Rights.

mcqs.q: Article 14 guarantees:
mcqs.explanation: Article 14: equality before law and equal protection of laws.

mcqs.q: Right to Education was added as Article 21A by which amendment?
mcqs.explanation: The 86th Amendment (2002) made free, compulsory education (6-14 years) a fundamental right.

mcqs.q: How many freedoms are guaranteed under Article 19?
mcqs.explanation: Article 19 gives six freedoms — speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession.

mcqs.q: Right to Constitutional Remedies is guaranteed by:
mcqs.explanation: Article 32 (Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution) lets citizens move the Supreme Court directly.

mcqs.q: Which Article prohibits untouchability?
mcqs.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability in any form.

mcqs.q: Right against exploitation is covered by Articles:
mcqs.explanation: Articles 23 (traffic in humans, forced labour) and 24 (child labour in hazardous work).

mcqs.q: Which right was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment?
mcqs.explanation: The 44th Amendment (1978) moved property to Article 300A — a legal right, not fundamental.

mcqs.q: Cultural and educational rights are given in Articles:
mcqs.explanation: Articles 29-30 protect minority language, culture and institutions.

mcqs.q: Freedom of religion is guaranteed by Articles:
mcqs.explanation: Articles 25-28 give freedom of conscience and free profession/practice of religion.

mcqs.q: The writ 'Mandamus' means:
mcqs.explanation: Mandamus orders a public official to perform a mandatory duty.

mcqs.q: Equality of opportunity in public employment is guaranteed by:
mcqs.explanation: Article 16 ensures equal opportunity in government jobs.

mcqs.q: Which Article protects life and personal liberty?
mcqs.explanation: Article 21: no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by legal procedure.

mcqs.q: Fundamental Rights are enforceable against:
options: the State primarily (and some against private persons)
mcqs.explanation: They are primarily guarantees against State action (Article 12 defines 'State').

mcqs.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in —
mcqs.explanation: DPSPs occupy Part IV of the Constitution, covering Articles 36 to 51; Fundamental Duties are Part IV-A (Art 51A).

mcqs.q: Article 40 of the Constitution directs the State to —
mcqs.explanation: Article 40, a Gandhian principle, directs the State to organise village panchayats; it became the base for the 73rd Amendment.

mcqs.q: Free legal aid is provided under which Article?
mcqs.explanation: Article 39A (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976) mandates equal justice and free legal aid; Lok Adalats flow from it.

mcqs.q: How many Fundamental Duties does Article 51A contain at present?
mcqs.explanation: Originally 10 duties under Article 51A (42nd Amendment, 1976); the 11th — Article 51A(k), education of 6-14 children — was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

mcqs.q: Which Article separates the judiciary from the executive in public services?
mcqs.explanation: Article 50 (Liberal-Intellectual DPSP) directs separation of judiciary from executive in public services.

mcqs.q: The idea of Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution is borrowed from —
mcqs.explanation: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) follow the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR; DPSPs follow Ireland; FRs follow the USA.

mcqs.q: Which amendment converted Article 45 from "free education" to "early childhood care"?
mcqs.explanation: The 86th Amendment (2002) shifted free education (6-14 yrs) to new Article 21A and re-titled Article 45 for early childhood care below 6 years.

mcqs.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which part of the Constitution?
mcqs.explanation: DPSP are in Part IV (Articles 36-51).

mcqs.q: How many Fundamental Duties are there in the Indian Constitution currently?
mcqs.explanation: Originally 10 duties added by 42nd Amendment; 11th (duty to provide education opportunities to children 6-14) added by 86th Amendment (2002).

mcqs.q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the Uniform Civil Code?
mcqs.explanation: Article 44 directs the State to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout India.

mcqs.q: The Fundamental Duties are contained in:
mcqs.explanation: Fundamental Duties are in Part IV-A (Article 51A), added by 42nd Amendment (1976).

mcqs.q: The Directive Principles are:
mcqs.explanation: DPSP are non-justiciable — courts cannot enforce them but they are 'fundamental in the governance of the country' (Art 37).

mcqs.q: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended:
mcqs.explanation: The Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended the inclusion of Fundamental Duties in the Constitution.

mcqs.q: Which Article promotes free legal aid?
mcqs.explanation: Article 39A directs the State to secure free legal aid to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

mcqs.q: Which Article directs the State to organize Village Panchayats?
mcqs.explanation: Article 40 directs the State to organize Village Panchayats and endow them with powers to function as units of self-government.

mcqs.q: The 'living wage' for workers is mentioned in:
mcqs.explanation: Article 43 directs the State to secure a living wage and decent conditions of work for workers.

mcqs.q: Separation of Judiciary from Executive is provided under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 50 directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.

mcqs.q: Promotion of international peace and security is mentioned in:
mcqs.explanation: Article 51 directs the State to promote international peace and security, maintain just relations between nations, and respect international law.

mcqs.q: The 11th Fundamental Duty added by 86th Amendment (2002) relates to:
mcqs.explanation: The 86th Amendment (2002) added Art 51A(k) — duty of parents/guardians to provide opportunities for education to children aged 6-14 years.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a category of Directive Principles?
mcqs.explanation: DPSP have three categories: Socialist, Gandhian, and Liberal-Intellectual. 'Conservative' is not a category.

mcqs.q: Article 44 directs the State to enact:
mcqs.explanation: Article 44 — Uniform Civil Code.

mcqs.q: Article 50 directs separation of:
mcqs.explanation: Article 50 — separation of judiciary from executive.

mcqs.q: Who recommended Fundamental Duties?
mcqs.explanation: Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended Fundamental Duties.

mcqs.q: DPSP promote what kind of welfare state?
options: Welfare state with social and economic justice
mcqs.explanation: DPSP aim to establish welfare state with social, economic, political justice.

mcqs.q: The 11th Fundamental Duty was added in:
mcqs.explanation: 11th Fundamental Duty (education to children 6-14) added by 86th Amendment (2002).

mcqs.q: Number of Directive Principles in Part IV:
mcqs.explanation: Articles 36-51 contain approximately 15 DPSPs.

mcqs.q: Protection of environment is:
mcqs.explanation: 51A(g) — Fundamental Duty to protect environment; also Article 48A (DPSP).

mcqs.q: Free and compulsory education for children is directed in Article:
mcqs.explanation: Article 45 — originally free and compulsory education for children 6-14; now after 86th Amendment, Article 21A made it Fundamental Right.

mcqs.q: Promotion of cottage industries is in Article:
mcqs.explanation: Article 43 — promote cottage industries; suitable working conditions.

mcqs.q: Promotion of educational interests of weaker sections is in Article:
mcqs.explanation: Article 46 — promote educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, weaker sections.

mcqs.q: Protection of monuments and places of national importance is in Article:
mcqs.explanation: Article 49 — protection of monuments and places of national importance.

mcqs.q: Safeguard forests and wild animals is in Article:
mcqs.explanation: Article 48A — safeguard forests and wildlife (added by 42nd Amendment, 1976).

mcqs.q: Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in:
mcqs.explanation: Part IV (Articles 36-51) contains the DPSP.

mcqs.q: DPSPs are borrowed from the Constitution of:
mcqs.explanation: Ireland inspired the Directive Principles (Spanish Constitution also had precedents).

mcqs.q: Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) is a:
mcqs.explanation: UCC is a DPSP — the State shall endeavour to secure it.

mcqs.q: Fundamental Duties were added by which amendment?
mcqs.explanation: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Part IVA with Fundamental Duties on Swaran Singh Committee advice.

mcqs.q: How many Fundamental Duties are listed in Article 51A today?
mcqs.explanation: Originally 10; the 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th (education of children 6-14).

mcqs.q: Which DPSP article promotes prohibition of intoxicants?
mcqs.explanation: Article 47 directs raising nutrition levels and prohibiting intoxicating drinks/drugs.

mcqs.q: Article 51 relates to:
options: promotion of international peace and security
mcqs.explanation: Article 51: foster respect for international law, treaty obligations, and peace.

mcqs.q: DPSPs differ from Fundamental Rights because they are:
mcqs.explanation: DPSPs guide governance but cannot be enforced by courts; FRs are justiciable.

mcqs.q: The first Fundamental Duty requires citizens to abide by:
options: the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and Anthem
mcqs.explanation: Article 51A(a) — respect the Constitution, Flag and Anthem.

mcqs.q: Which committee recommended Fundamental Duties?
mcqs.explanation: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) suggested adding Fundamental Duties.

mcqs.q: Article 39A directs the State to provide:
options: free legal aid and equal justice
mcqs.explanation: Article 39A: equal justice and free legal aid (42nd Amendment).

mcqs.q: Which Article directs protection and improvement of the environment?
mcqs.explanation: Article 48A (42nd Amendment) — protect environment, forests and wildlife.

mcqs.q: Minerva Mills case (1980) established that:
options: Judicial review and the FR-DPSP balance form the basic structure
Preamble is not part of Constitution
mcqs.explanation: It struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment, reinforcing the basic structure doctrine.

mcqs.q: The President of India is elected by —
options: Elected MPs and elected MLAs including Delhi & Puducherry
mcqs.explanation: Articles 54-55: electoral college = elected MPs + elected MLAs of states; the 70th Amendment added elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry.

mcqs.q: The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of —
mcqs.explanation: Under Article 64 the Vice-President acts as ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).

mcqs.q: Impeachment of the President requires a majority of —
options: 2/3rd present and voting in Lok Sabha
2/3rd of total membership of both Houses
mcqs.explanation: Article 61: charge for "violation of the Constitution" passed by 2/3rd of the TOTAL membership of each House.

mcqs.q: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of —
mcqs.explanation: Article 117(1): Money Bills need the President's prior recommendation and are introduced only in the Lok Sabha.

mcqs.q: The quorum in either House of Parliament is —
mcqs.explanation: Article 100(3): quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, including the presiding officer.

mcqs.q: Which Article establishes the Parliament of India?
mcqs.explanation: Article 79: Parliament consists of the President, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

mcqs.q: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to —
mcqs.explanation: Article 75(3) — the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; a no-confidence motion removes it.

mcqs.q: Who is the executive head of the Indian State?
mcqs.explanation: President of India is the executive head of the State (Article 53). Prime Minister is head of the government/council of ministers.

mcqs.q: The President of India is elected by:
options: Electoral College consisting of elected MPs and MLAs
mcqs.explanation: President is elected indirectly by an Electoral College (Art 54) consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States & UTs (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K).

mcqs.q: The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of:
mcqs.explanation: The Vice-President (Art 63) is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Art 64).

mcqs.q: The Parliament of India consists of:
mcqs.explanation: Article 79: Parliament = President + Lok Sabha (House of the People) + Rajya Sabha (Council of States).

mcqs.q: What is the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha as per the Constitution?
mcqs.explanation: Maximum 550 members (530 from States + 20 from UTs). Current strength is 543.

mcqs.q: The Rajya Sabha is:
mcqs.explanation: Rajya Sabha is a permanent body — it is never dissolved. 1/3 of its members retire every 2 years.

mcqs.q: The term of a member of Rajya Sabha is:
mcqs.explanation: Each Rajya Sabha member serves a 6-year term; 1/3 retire every 2 years ensuring continuity.

mcqs.q: Money Bills can be introduced in:
mcqs.explanation: Article 109: Money Bills can only be introduced in Lok Sabha. Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments within 14 days; Lok Sabha may accept or reject.

mcqs.q: The President can promulgate an Ordinance under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 123: President can promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session. Valid for 6 months + 6 weeks.

mcqs.q: The minimum age to contest for the post of President of India is:
mcqs.explanation: Article 58: To be eligible for President, a person must be a citizen of India, 35+ years, and qualified to be a member of Lok Sabha.

mcqs.q: Who appoints the Prime Minister of India?
mcqs.explanation: Article 75: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President. The PM must be a member of either House of Parliament.

mcqs.q: The strength of the Rajya Sabha is limited to a maximum of:
mcqs.explanation: Article 80: Maximum 250 members (238 elected + 12 nominated by President). Currently 245.

mcqs.q: How many members are nominated by the President to the Rajya Sabha?
mcqs.explanation: 12 members are nominated by the President for their expertise in literature, science, art, and social service.

mcqs.q: A person must be at least how old to become a member of Lok Sabha?
mcqs.explanation: Article 84: Minimum age for Lok Sabha is 25 years; for Rajya Sabha it is 30 years.

mcqs.q: A Money Bill passed by Lok Sabha is returned by Rajya Sabha within:
mcqs.explanation: Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days with or without recommendations.

mcqs.q: The minimum age prescribed for becoming President of India is — (हिंदी: राष्ट्रपति के लिए न्यूनतम आयु?)
mcqs.explanation: Article 58 requires 35 years for President; the corresponding ages are 25 for Lok Sabha and 30 for Rajya Sabha membership.

mcqs.q: The President of India addresses his/her resignation letter to —
mcqs.explanation: The President resigns by writing to the Vice-President; the Vice-President in turn resigns to the President.

mcqs.q: If both the President and the Vice-President are unavailable, who discharges the functions of the President?
mcqs.explanation: By convention under Article 65, when neither the President nor the Vice-President is available, the Chief Justice of India acts as President.

mcqs.q: The 61st Constitutional Amendment (1989) lowered the voting age from 21 years to —
mcqs.explanation: The 61st Amendment amended Article 326 to grant universal adult franchise at 18 years, effective from 1989.

mcqs.q: The term of a Rajya Sabha member is — (हिंदी: राज्यसभा सदस्य का कार्यकाल?)
mcqs.explanation: A Rajya Sabha member serves 6 years, with one-third of members retiring every two years; the House itself is never dissolved.

mcqs.q: The minimum age for membership of the Lok Sabha is —
mcqs.explanation: Lok Sabha candidates must be at least 25 years old (Article 84); the Rajya Sabha requires 30 years.

mcqs.q: The Estimates Committee of Parliament consists of —
options: 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha
22 members, all from the Rajya Sabha
mcqs.explanation: The Estimates Committee has 30 members elected only from the Lok Sabha; the 22-member Public Accounts Committee mixes both Houses (15 LS + 7 RS).

mcqs.q: Which Parliamentary committee is, by convention, chaired by a member of the Opposition?
mcqs.explanation: The Public Accounts Committee is conventionally headed by an opposition MP, while the Estimates Committee is chaired by a ruling-party member.

mcqs.q: A joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament is presided over by —
options: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
mcqs.explanation: Under Article 118(4), the Speaker presides over joint sittings (held only thrice — 1961, 1978, 2002), followed by the Deputy Speaker and then the Deputy Chairman RS.

mcqs.q: Who was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
mcqs.explanation: Ganesh Vasudev Mavalankar, Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly from 1946, became the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha in 1952.

mcqs.q: A no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers can be moved —
options: In either House with 50 members’ support
Only in the Lok Sabha with the support of 50 members
Only in the Rajya Sabha with the President’s consent
In the Lok Sabha only with the Speaker’s prior permission
mcqs.explanation: Under Rule 198, a no-confidence motion is allowed only in the Lok Sabha and needs the leave of the House supported by at least 50 members.

mcqs.q: "Zero Hour" in Parliament begins —
options: At the end of the day’s sitting
mcqs.explanation: Zero Hour starts at 12 noon right after the Question Hour — an Indian innovation not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.

mcqs.q: The Vice-President of India is elected by —
options: All members (elected + nominated) of both Houses of Parliament
Elected members of the Lok Sabha only
Lok Sabha members and State Legislative Assemblies
mcqs.explanation: Article 66: the Vice-President’s electoral college consists of ALL members — elected and nominated — of both Houses; no state MLAs take part.

mcqs.q: The President can nominate how many members to the Rajya Sabha from art, literature, science and social service?
mcqs.explanation: Article 80 lets the President nominate 12 persons with special knowledge to the Rajya Sabha (maximum strength 250 = 238 + 12).

mcqs.q: Under the Constitution, a person can be re-elected as President of India —
mcqs.explanation: Article 57 places no bar on the number of re-elections; Dr. Rajendra Prasad in fact served two consecutive terms.

mcqs.q: The Supreme Court of India was established under which Article?
mcqs.explanation: Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court with a CJI and other judges; it replaced the Federal Court on 26 January 1950.

mcqs.q: A judge of the Supreme Court retires at the age of —
mcqs.explanation: Supreme Court judges hold office till 65 years (Article 124); High Court judges till 62 years (Article 217).

mcqs.q: Disputes between two states (e.g., river water) are decided under the Supreme Court's —
mcqs.explanation: Article 131 grants exclusive original jurisdiction to the SC in Centre-State and inter-state disputes.

mcqs.q: Which Article makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts?
mcqs.explanation: Article 141: the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India; Article 142 allows decrees for complete justice.

mcqs.q: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 is —
mcqs.explanation: Article 226 allows writs for Fundamental Rights AND "any other purpose", making it wider than Article 32.

mcqs.q: The NJAC Act and 99th Constitutional Amendment were struck down by the Supreme Court in —
mcqs.explanation: In October 2015 (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association case), the SC struck down the 99th Amendment to Articles 124 & 217, holding the NJAC violated judicial independence (basic structure).

mcqs.q: Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is invoked by —
mcqs.explanation: Under Article 143 the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion; the opinion is advisory, not binding.

mcqs.q: The Supreme Court of India came into existence on:
mcqs.explanation: Supreme Court came into existence on 28 January 1950 (two days after the Constitution came into effect).

mcqs.q: The current sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court (including CJI) is:
mcqs.explanation: In 2019, the strength was increased from 31 to 34 (1 CJI + 33 other judges).

mcqs.q: The retirement age of a Supreme Court judge is:
mcqs.explanation: Supreme Court judges retire at 65 years; High Court judges at 62.

mcqs.q: A High Court judge retires at the age of:
mcqs.explanation: High Court judges retire at 62 years; Supreme Court judges at 65.

mcqs.q: The first Chief Justice of India was:
mcqs.explanation: Sir Harilal Jekisundas Kania was the first CJI (1950-1951).

mcqs.q: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is under which Article?
mcqs.explanation: Article 143: President may seek the Supreme Court's opinion on any question of law or fact of public importance.

mcqs.q: The Special Leave to Appeal is granted by the Supreme Court under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 136: Supreme Court may grant Special Leave to Appeal from any judgment of any court or tribunal (except military).

mcqs.q: The writ jurisdiction of the High Court is provided under:
mcqs.explanation: Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction than Article 32 (SC) — HCs can issue writs for any purpose, not just Fundamental Rights.

mcqs.q: The number of High Courts in India is currently:
mcqs.explanation: There are 25 High Courts in India (after Telangana HC separated from Andhra Pradesh HC in 2019).

mcqs.q: The first High Court in India was established at:
mcqs.explanation: The Calcutta High Court was established on 1 July 1862 — first HC in India.

mcqs.q: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India was pioneered by:
mcqs.explanation: Justice P.N. Bhagwati is credited with introducing PIL concept — allows public-spirited individuals to file on behalf of those who cannot.

mcqs.q: The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction extends to:
options: Disputes between Government of India and States
mcqs.explanation: Article 131: Original jurisdiction covers disputes between Centre and States, or between two or more States.

mcqs.q: A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed by:
options: Impeachment by special majority of both Houses
mcqs.explanation: Article 124(4): A judge can be removed by impeachment — special majority of both Houses — on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

mcqs.q: The Public Interest Litigation can be filed in:
options: Both Supreme Court and High Court
mcqs.explanation: PIL can be filed under Article 32 (SC) for Fundamental Rights OR under Article 226 (HC) for any matter including FRs.

mcqs.q: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
mcqs.explanation: Article 32 — 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution (Dr. Ambedkar).

mcqs.q: The first woman judge of the Supreme Court of India was:
mcqs.explanation: Justice Fathima Beevi (1989) — first woman judge of SC; appointed by President R. Venkataraman.

mcqs.q: The current CJI (2024-25) Justice Sanjiv Khanna is the ___ CJI of India.
mcqs.explanation: Justice Sanjiv Khanna is the 51st CJI of India (since 11 November 2024).

mcqs.q: The landmark Keshavananda Bharati case (1973) was about:
mcqs.explanation: Keshavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973) — SC propounded 'Basic Structure Doctrine' — Parliament cannot alter basic structure.

mcqs.q: The minimum number of judges required for a Constitutional Bench of SC is:
mcqs.explanation: Constitutional Bench of SC has minimum 5 judges; larger benches of 7, 9, 11 for important cases.

mcqs.q: The High Court with jurisdiction over maximum states is:
mcqs.explanation: Guwahati High Court — had jurisdiction over all 7 NE states till 2018-19; now only Assam after separate HCs created.

mcqs.q: 'Public Interest Litigation' (PIL) can be filed by:
mcqs.explanation: PIL — any public-spirited person can file on behalf of affected; concept introduced by Justice P.N. Bhagwati.
